# Part 1: Discriminant Validity {#sec-part1}

## The Classical Test Theory Starting Point

Every measurement model in the social sciences begins from the same core assumption: the observed score you record is a sum of the *true* score and *measurement error*.

$$X_\text{observed} = T_\text{true} + \varepsilon$$

Classical test theory (CTT) assumes the error term $\varepsilon$ is *random and symmetric*: equally likely to push the observed score up or down, averaging to zero. Under this assumption, observed scores are noisy but unbiased indicators of the latent construct you care about.

But this assumption is almost always violated in practice. The measurement error is not symmetric; it is contaminated by *something else*. The {{< nparts >}} parts in this tutorial are {{< nparts >}} different ways that "something else" creeps into your observed score:

- When your scale picks up a second construct (**{{< ref sec-discriminant-validity style="part" >}}**), ε includes that construct's variance and is no longer random.
- When an omitted variable drives both your predictor and outcome (**{{< ref sec-omitted-variable-bias style="part" >}}**), the "error" in your regression coefficient is systematic, not random.
- When scale items shift their baseline across groups (**{{< ref sec-measurement-invariance style="part" >}}**), ε differs systematically between conditions.
- When your sample mixes two populations (**{{< ref sec-latent-subgroups style="part" >}}**), ε has a bimodal structure that standard models cannot represent.
- When your data contain influential outliers (**{{< ref sec-outliers style="part" >}}**), ε includes extreme values that disproportionately distort regression coefficients.
- When your outcome scale has hard bounds (**{{< ref sec-bounded-scales style="part" >}}**), ε is truncated at the ends of the scale, so observed means are pulled toward the middle.

**Discriminant validity failure is the case where the error in your observed scale is not random noise but structured variance from a second latent construct.** Suppose we are trying to measure Green Purchase Intentions (GPI), but our measure also captures a related construct, Environmental Concern (EC). Then the CTT equation becomes

$$X_\text{GPI} = T_\text{true GPI} + \lambda \cdot T_\text{EC} + \varepsilon_\text{random},$$

where $\lambda$ is how much Environmental Concern bleeds into your GPI items. This is no longer a pure measure of one construct.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The same problem in other disciplines

The same issue, an observable index picking up several latent sources of variance, appears under different names across fields:

- **Econometrics / identification**: a coefficient is *unidentified* when the predictor of interest cannot be separated from another variable that moves with it.
- **Epidemiology**: a biomarker elevated by both inflammation *and* metabolic syndrome lacks *specificity*.
- **Psychometrics**: *construct contamination* (the scale measures variance beyond the intended construct); its mirror image is *construct deficiency*.
- **Political science**: composite indices (democracy, corruption) often collapse several dimensions into one number.

Whenever a single observed variable (or a scale) proxies a latent construct, you need to verify it is specific to *that* construct.
:::

## The Study Scenario

We simulate a **green marketing experiment** with 400 participants, asking whether eco-friendly brand messaging increases green purchase intentions. Half saw standard product advertising (**Control**); half saw ads emphasising eco-friendly credentials (**Green Marketing**). All constructs are measured on 7-point Likert scales:

| Construct | Abbreviation | # Items | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Environmental Concern | EC | 4 | Covariate |
| Green Purchase Intention | GPI | 4 | Dependent Variable |
| Brand Attitude | BA | 3 | Covariate |

**The hidden problem we planted:** the GPI items are nearly indistinguishable from the EC items (the latent correlation is 0.93). Any effect of the campaign on GPI is then hard to interpret: are participants more willing to buy, or just more environmentally concerned? In all {{< nparts >}} parts, the core problem is the same: the **observed Y** is an imperfect, contaminated proxy for the **latent Y** you want to study.

::: {.callout-important}
## These statistical tests only apply in specific situations

Discriminant validity is a concern whenever two related constructs are in your study, but the tests below (HTMT and DVI) require **multi-item Likert scales with at least four items per construct**. They do *not* apply to single-item outcomes, willingness to pay, choice data, or behavior. If your DV is one of those, discriminant validity is still your responsibility; it is just harder to detect, and the last section of this part covers what to do.
:::

## Simulating the Data

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Simulation details and descriptives

We use `MASS::mvrnorm()` to generate correlated latent factor scores, create item scores from those factors plus random error, and round to a 7-point scale. EC and GPI are correlated at **0.93** in the population, well above the 0.90 threshold used in HTMT-based tests ([Henseler et al., 2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8)).

```{r simulate-data}
#| code-summary: "▶ Simulate green marketing dataset (n=400)"
set.seed(2025)
n <- 400

# ── Step 1: Assign participants to conditions ──────────────────────────────────
treatment <- sample(c(0L, 1L), size = n, replace = TRUE)

# ── Step 2: Define the true factor correlation matrix ─────────────────────────
# EC and GPI are correlated at .93 — too high for discriminant validity
# EC–BA and GPI–BA are at more typical, moderate levels
phi_pop <- matrix(
  c(1.00, 0.93, 0.45,   # EC row
    0.93, 1.00, 0.50,   # GPI row
    0.45, 0.50, 1.00),  # BA row
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("EC", "GPI", "BA"), c("EC", "GPI", "BA"))
)

# ── Step 3: Generate latent factor scores ─────────────────────────────────────
latent_base <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = n, mu = c(0, 0, 0), Sigma = phi_pop)

EC_lat  <- latent_base[, 1]
GPI_lat <- latent_base[, 2] + 0.40 * treatment  # Green marketing raises GPI by .40 SD
BA_lat  <- latent_base[, 3]

# ── Step 4: Define item loadings ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# These represent how strongly each item reflects its latent construct
lambda_EC  <- c(0.78, 0.82, 0.74, 0.76)
lambda_GPI <- c(0.80, 0.76, 0.82, 0.78)
lambda_BA  <- c(0.72, 0.76, 0.70)

# ── Step 5: Generate continuous item scores (latent score + measurement error) ─
gen_items <- function(latent, loadings) {
  sapply(loadings, function(lam) {
    lam * latent + sqrt(1 - lam^2) * rnorm(length(latent))
  })
}

EC_cont  <- gen_items(EC_lat,  lambda_EC)
GPI_cont <- gen_items(GPI_lat, lambda_GPI)
BA_cont  <- gen_items(BA_lat,  lambda_BA)

# ── Step 6: Round to 7-point Likert scale ─────────────────────────────────────
# Cut the continuous distribution into 7 ordered categories
to_likert7 <- function(x) {
  z <- (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)   # standardise each item
  breaks <- c(-Inf, -1.5, -0.75, -0.25, 0.25, 0.75, 1.5, Inf)
  as.integer(cut(z, breaks = breaks, labels = 1:7))
}

EC_lik  <- apply(EC_cont,  2, to_likert7)
GPI_lik <- apply(GPI_cont, 2, to_likert7)
BA_lik  <- apply(BA_cont,  2, to_likert7)

# ── Step 7: Assemble the final data frame ─────────────────────────────────────
df <- data.frame(
  id        = 1:n,
  condition = factor(treatment, levels = c(0, 1),
                     labels = c("Control", "Green Marketing")),
  EC1  = EC_lik[, 1], EC2  = EC_lik[, 2],
  EC3  = EC_lik[, 3], EC4  = EC_lik[, 4],
  GPI1 = GPI_lik[, 1], GPI2 = GPI_lik[, 2],
  GPI3 = GPI_lik[, 3], GPI4 = GPI_lik[, 4],
  BA1  = BA_lik[, 1], BA2  = BA_lik[, 2], BA3  = BA_lik[, 3]
)

# Quick look at the data
head(df, 5)
```

```{r describe-data}
#| code-summary: "▶ Descriptive statistics by condition"
# Count participants per condition and compute scale means
df |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  summarise(
    n          = n(),
    Mean_EC    = round(rowMeans(across(EC1:EC4))  |> mean(), 2),
    Mean_GPI   = round(rowMeans(across(GPI1:GPI4)) |> mean(), 2),
    Mean_BA    = round(rowMeans(across(BA1:BA3))  |> mean(), 2)
  ) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Condition", "N", "Mean EC", "Mean GPI", "Mean BA"),
        caption = "Sample sizes and scale means by condition")
```

The manipulation works as intended: GPI is higher in the green marketing condition than in control.
:::::

## First Look: Convergent and Discriminant Validity in the Raw Data

Before any formal test, look at the raw correlation structure of the 11 items. **Convergent validity**: items within a scale should correlate strongly. **Discriminant validity**: items from *different* scales should correlate noticeably less. The warning sign is a between-scale block that looks as dark as the within-scale blocks.

```{r correlation-heatmap, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 7}
#| code-summary: "▶ Plot: item correlation heatmap"
# Extract just the item columns (no ID or condition)
items_df <- df |> select(EC1:BA3)

# Compute correlation matrix
item_cors <- cor(items_df)

# Color-coded heatmap
# Warm colors = high positive correlation; cool colors = low/negative
corrplot(item_cors,
         method   = "color",
         type     = "lower",
         order    = "original",     # keep original order so EC, GPI, BA stay grouped
         tl.col   = "black",
         tl.cex   = 0.85,
         addCoef.col = "white",     # print correlation values
         number.cex  = 0.65,
         col      = colorRampPalette(c("#313695", "#74add1", "#e0f3f8",
                                       "#fee090", "#f46d43", "#a50026"))(200),
         title    = "Item Correlation Matrix",
         mar      = c(0, 0, 1.5, 0))
```

The EC–EC and GPI–GPI blocks are high, as they should be. But the **EC–GPI block is just as high**, so the two scales cannot be told apart. The table summarizes the same thing in numbers.

```{r htmt-illustration}
#| code-summary: "▶ Compute average within- and between-scale correlations"
# Compute average correlations within each scale and between scales
cors <- cor(items_df)

within_EC  <- mean(cors[1:4, 1:4][lower.tri(cors[1:4, 1:4])])
within_GPI <- mean(cors[5:8, 5:8][lower.tri(cors[5:8, 5:8])])
within_BA  <- mean(cors[9:11, 9:11][lower.tri(cors[9:11, 9:11])])

between_EC_GPI <- mean(abs(cors[1:4, 5:8]))
between_EC_BA  <- mean(abs(cors[1:4, 9:11]))
between_GPI_BA <- mean(abs(cors[5:8, 9:11]))

avg_cor_summary <- data.frame(
  Type  = c("Within EC",  "Within GPI", "Within BA",
            "Between EC–GPI ⚠️", "Between EC–BA", "Between GPI–BA"),
  Avg_r = round(c(within_EC, within_GPI, within_BA,
                  between_EC_GPI, between_EC_BA, between_GPI_BA), 3)
)
kable(avg_cor_summary, col.names = c("Correlation Type", "Average |r|"),
      caption = "Average within-scale and between-scale correlations")
```

EC items correlate with each other at about `r sprintf("%.2f", within_EC)`, GPI items at about `r sprintf("%.2f", within_GPI)`, and EC with GPI items at about `r sprintf("%.2f", between_EC_GPI)`. Knowing someone's EC score tells you almost as much about their GPI items as their own GPI scores do. The HTMT ratio formalises exactly this comparison: if within- and between-scale correlations are similar, HTMT is close to 1.

## Factor Analysis and Convergent Validity {#sec-factor-analysis}

Factor analysis starts from the same CTT logic: each item is a noisy reflection of a latent construct plus error. **Exploratory** factor analysis (EFA) lets the data reveal how many factors are needed; **confirmatory** factor analysis (CFA) tests a specific, theory-driven structure. Both ask the convergent validity question: *do the items meant to measure the same construct cluster together?*

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Exploratory factor analysis (scree plot, loadings, variance explained)

EFA makes no assumption about which items belong together. **Parallel analysis** compares your eigenvalues to those from random data of the same size; retain factors only where your eigenvalue clearly exceeds the random baseline.

```{r efa-parallel, fig.height=5, fig.width=8}
#| code-summary: "▶ Scree plot with parallel analysis"
# fa.parallel() overlays observed eigenvalues on eigenvalues from 200 randomly
# generated datasets of the same size. Points where the observed line (solid)
# sits clearly above the random baseline (dashed) indicate real factors.
fa.parallel(
  items_df,
  fa          = "fa",    # factor analysis (not principal components)
  fm          = "ml",    # maximum likelihood extraction
  n.iter      = 200,     # random datasets for the parallel baseline
  main        = "Scree Plot with Parallel Analysis",
  show.legend = TRUE
)
```

With 11 items designed as three constructs we hope to see three factors. Because EC and GPI are simulated with a 0.93 correlation, the data may clearly support only two, and that ambiguity is itself a warning about discriminant validity.

We then extract three factors with **oblique rotation** (`oblimin`), which lets factors correlate, as constructs in one survey typically do.

```{r efa-loadings}
#| code-summary: "▶ EFA with 3 factors (oblique rotation)"
efa_fit <- fa(
  items_df,
  nfactors = 3,           # number of factors to extract
  rotate   = "oblimin",   # oblique rotation — allows correlated factors
  fm       = "ml",        # maximum likelihood estimation
  scores   = "regression"
)

# Print loadings; values below 0.30 suppressed to highlight the pattern
print(loadings(efa_fit), cutoff = 0.30, sort = FALSE)
```

Loadings above 0.40 are meaningful and above 0.70 strong. Good convergent validity means EC items load on one factor, GPI items on another, and BA items on a third. Here GPI items may also load on the EC factor (*cross-loading*), the factor-analytic signature of discriminant validity failure.

```{r efa-variance-table}
#| code-summary: "▶ Variance explained by each factor"
efa_var <- data.frame(
  Factor      = paste0("Factor ", 1:3),
  SS_Loadings = round(efa_fit$Vaccounted["SS loadings",     ], 3),
  Prop_Var    = round(efa_fit$Vaccounted["Proportion Var",  ], 3),
  Cum_Var     = round(efa_fit$Vaccounted["Cumulative Var",  ], 3)
)
kable(efa_var,
      col.names = c("Factor", "SS Loadings",
                    "Proportion of Variance", "Cumulative Variance"),
      caption   = "EFA: variance explained by each factor")
```
:::::

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Confirmatory factor analysis (fit indices, loadings)

CFA imposes the structure you designed: EC items load only on EC, GPI only on GPI, BA only on BA. The question is how well that constrained model fits.

| Index | What it measures | Good fit |
|---|---|---|
| **CFI** | Improvement over a null model | ≥ 0.95 |
| **TLI** | Like CFI; penalises complexity | ≥ 0.95 |
| **RMSEA** | Absolute discrepancy per degree of freedom | ≤ 0.06 |
| **SRMR** | Average residual correlation | ≤ 0.08 |

Standardised loadings above 0.50 are acceptable and above 0.70 strong.

```{r cfa-convergent}
#| code-summary: "▶ CFA: test the hypothesised 3-factor structure"
cfa_model_conv <- '
  EC  =~ EC1 + EC2 + EC3 + EC4
  GPI =~ GPI1 + GPI2 + GPI3 + GPI4
  BA  =~ BA1  + BA2  + BA3
'

# std.lv = TRUE: fixes factor variances to 1 so loadings and factor
# correlations are directly interpretable on a standardised scale
fit_conv <- cfa(cfa_model_conv, data = items_df, std.lv = TRUE)
summary(fit_conv, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
```

```{r cfa-std-loadings}
#| code-summary: "▶ Standardised factor loadings table"
std_loads <- standardizedSolution(fit_conv) |>
  filter(op == "=~") |>
  select(lhs, rhs, est.std, se, pvalue) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

kable(std_loads,
      col.names = c("Construct", "Item", "Std. Loading", "SE", "p-value"),
      caption   = "CFA standardised factor loadings — convergent validity evidence")
```

```{r cfa-fit-table}
#| code-summary: "▶ Fit indices summary"
fi <- fitMeasures(fit_conv,
      c("cfi","tli","rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower","rmsea.ci.upper","srmr"))

fit_summary <- data.frame(
  Index     = c("CFI","TLI","RMSEA","RMSEA 90% CI","SRMR"),
  Value     = c(round(fi["cfi"],  3),
                round(fi["tli"],  3),
                round(fi["rmsea"],3),
                paste0("[", round(fi["rmsea.ci.lower"],3),
                       ", ", round(fi["rmsea.ci.upper"],3), "]"),
                round(fi["srmr"], 3)),
  Benchmark = c("≥ 0.95","≥ 0.95","≤ 0.06","—","≤ 0.08")
)
kable(fit_summary,
      col.names = c("Fit Index","Value","Good Fit Benchmark"),
      caption   = "CFA model fit indices")
```
:::::

::: {.callout-warning}
## What the results reveal: a two-part story

**Convergent validity is fine.** Loadings are strong (> 0.70) for EC, GPI, and BA items; the items cohere within each scale.

**Discriminant validity is not.** The EC and GPI factors correlate at about 0.93 (the `~~` rows in the CFA `summary()`). Convergent and discriminant validity are distinct assessments and can give opposite verdicts: items can hang together within each scale while the scales themselves remain statistically indistinguishable.
:::

## Discriminant Validity Testing Methods {#sec-dv-methods}

The items converge within their intended scales. The question now is whether the scales can be *distinguished from each other*. Two formal methods are available for multi-item Likert scales. The explanation of each is below; running it in R is in the dropdown.

### Method 1: HTMT Analysis

HTMT is the **Heterotrait-Monotrait ratio of correlations**. *Monotrait* correlations are between items of the *same* scale; *heterotrait* correlations are between items of *different* scales. HTMT asks how large the between-scale correlations are relative to the within-scale ones. Near 1.0, the scales are not distinguishable.

- **HTMT < 0.85**: discriminant validity supported (strict)
- **HTMT < 0.90**: supported (lenient)
- **HTMT ≥ 0.90**: **violated**

We use **HTMT2**, the updated index based on the geometric mean of within-scale correlations, which is now recommended over the original.

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Run the HTMT analysis in R

`htmt()` needs a data frame of *only the scale items* (no IDs, condition, or demographics) and a model string in lavaan syntax.

```{r htmt-analysis}
#| code-summary: "▶ Run HTMT2 analysis"
# ── Model specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# This tells htmt() which items belong to which construct.
# It uses the same syntax as lavaan's CFA model specification.
cfa_model <- '
  EC  =~ EC1 + EC2 + EC3 + EC4
  GPI =~ GPI1 + GPI2 + GPI3 + GPI4
  BA  =~ BA1  + BA2  + BA3
'

# ── Run the HTMT analysis ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
htmt_result <- semTools::htmt(
  model    = cfa_model,   # factor structure: which items belong to which scale
  data     = items_df,    # item-level data ONLY (no id, no condition variable)
  htmt2    = TRUE,        # use HTMT2 (geometric mean) — recommended
  absolute = TRUE         # use absolute values of correlations
)

print(htmt_result)
```

| Argument | What it does | What to set |
|---|---|---|
| `model` | Which items belong to which construct | Same as your CFA syntax |
| `data` | Raw item data | Items only |
| `htmt2` | Original vs. updated formula | `TRUE` (recommended) |
| `absolute` | Absolute values of correlations | Keep `TRUE` |

```{r htmt-visualization, fig.height = 5}
#| code-summary: "▶ Plot: HTMT2 bar chart with thresholds"
# Extract the HTMT matrix and reshape for plotting
htmt_mat <- as.matrix(htmt_result)

# semTools fills only one triangle; we need a robust helper to extract a pair
get_htmt <- function(mat, r, c) {
  val <- mat[r, c]
  if (is.na(val)) val <- mat[c, r]   # try the other triangle
  as.numeric(val)
}

htmt_pairs <- data.frame(
  pair  = c("EC ↔ GPI", "EC ↔ BA", "GPI ↔ BA"),
  htmt  = c(get_htmt(htmt_mat, "EC", "GPI"),
            get_htmt(htmt_mat, "EC", "BA"),
            get_htmt(htmt_mat, "GPI", "BA")),
  label = c("Focal problem pair", "OK", "OK")
)

ggplot(htmt_pairs, aes(x = reorder(pair, -htmt), y = htmt, fill = label)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55, colour = "white") +
  # Threshold lines
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.90, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.85, linetype = "dotted",
             colour = "darkorange", linewidth = 0.9) +
  # Value labels on bars
  geom_text(aes(label = round(htmt, 3)), vjust = -0.5,
            fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  # Threshold annotations
  annotate("text", x = 3.45, y = 0.915,
           label = "Strict threshold (0.90)", colour = "firebrick",
           size = 3.3, hjust = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.45, y = 0.865,
           label = "Lenient threshold (0.85)", colour = "darkorange",
           size = 3.3, hjust = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Focal problem pair" = "#d73027",
                               "OK"                 = "#4575b4"),
                    name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.08), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "HTMT Value",
    title    = "HTMT2 Analysis: Discriminant Validity Check",
    subtitle = "Bars above the dashed line indicate discriminant validity concerns"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

**Reading the chart.** EC ↔ GPI exceeds both thresholds: a clear discriminant validity violation, so the GPI scale cannot be statistically distinguished from EC. EC ↔ BA and GPI ↔ BA are well below the thresholds. HTMT gives one number per pair and a rule of thumb; it ignores how *reliable* the scales are and offers no confidence interval, which is where the DVI comes in.
:::::

### Method 2: The DVI Method (Pieters et al., 2025)

HTMT is a good screen but has two gaps: its thresholds are rules of thumb, not formal tests, and it ignores scale reliability. A pair of highly reliable scales *should* be able to discriminate even when the factor correlation is somewhat high. Pieters et al. (2025) propose the **Discriminant Validity Index (DVI)**, which tests whether a scale's reliability is high enough, relative to the factor correlation, to support discriminant validity, in two steps.

**Step 1, the phi test:** is the factor correlation φ meaningfully below 1?

$$\text{DVI}_1 = 1 - |\phi|$$

If DVI₁ is not significantly above zero, stop: discriminant validity has failed.

**Step 2, the CR test:** even if φ < 1, is the scale reliable enough to "rise above" the factor correlation?

$$\text{DVI}_{CR} = \sqrt{CR} - |\phi|$$

where CR is the congeneric reliability (McDonald's omega). If DVI_CR > 0 with a confidence interval excluding zero, the scale can distinguish itself from the other construct. For example, with φ = 0.93 and CR = 0.83, √CR ≈ 0.91, which is below 0.93: DVI_CR is negative, and discriminant validity fails. Reliability sets an upper bound on how distinctly a scale can behave; if that bound is below the factor correlation, the scale is compromised.

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Run the DVI analysis in R (model, Wald and bootstrap CIs, forest plot, decision rule)

**Specify the model.** Define CR and DVI *inside* the lavaan syntax with the `:=` operator, so lavaan computes them and their standard errors. Every loading and error variance must be labelled, and the factor correlations too. `sqrt(phi^2)` takes the absolute value.

```{r dvi-model-spec}
#| code-summary: "▶ Specify the labeled CFA/DVI model"
dvi_model <- '
  # Measurement model
  EC  =~ lam_EC1*EC1 + lam_EC2*EC2 + lam_EC3*EC3 + lam_EC4*EC4
  GPI =~ lam_GPI1*GPI1 + lam_GPI2*GPI2 + lam_GPI3*GPI3 + lam_GPI4*GPI4
  BA  =~ lam_BA1*BA1 + lam_BA2*BA2 + lam_BA3*BA3

  # Error variances
  EC1  ~~ th_EC1*EC1
  EC2  ~~ th_EC2*EC2
  EC3  ~~ th_EC3*EC3
  EC4  ~~ th_EC4*EC4

  GPI1 ~~ th_GPI1*GPI1
  GPI2 ~~ th_GPI2*GPI2
  GPI3 ~~ th_GPI3*GPI3
  GPI4 ~~ th_GPI4*GPI4

  BA1  ~~ th_BA1*BA1
  BA2  ~~ th_BA2*BA2
  BA3  ~~ th_BA3*BA3

  # Factor correlations
  EC  ~~ phi_EC_GPI*GPI
  EC  ~~ phi_EC_BA*BA
  GPI ~~ phi_GPI_BA*BA

  # Congeneric reliability
  CR_EC  := ((lam_EC1 + lam_EC2 + lam_EC3 + lam_EC4)^2) / (((lam_EC1 + lam_EC2 + lam_EC3 + lam_EC4)^2) + th_EC1 + th_EC2 + th_EC3 + th_EC4)
  CR_GPI := ((lam_GPI1 + lam_GPI2 + lam_GPI3 + lam_GPI4)^2) / (((lam_GPI1 + lam_GPI2 + lam_GPI3 + lam_GPI4)^2) + th_GPI1 + th_GPI2 + th_GPI3 + th_GPI4)
  CR_BA  := ((lam_BA1 + lam_BA2 + lam_BA3)^2) / (((lam_BA1 + lam_BA2 + lam_BA3)^2) + th_BA1 + th_BA2 + th_BA3)

  # DVI
  DVI_1      := 1 - sqrt(phi_EC_GPI^2)
  DVI_CR_EC  := sqrt(CR_EC) - sqrt(phi_EC_GPI^2)
  DVI_CR_GPI := sqrt(CR_GPI) - sqrt(phi_EC_GPI^2)
'
```

**Fit it with `std.lv = TRUE`**, which fixes factor variances to 1 so that φ *is* a correlation. Without it, the covariance is on an arbitrary scale and DVI is not valid.

```{r cfa-fit}
#| code-summary: "▶ Fit CFA and get Wald confidence intervals"
# Fit the CFA using the labelled model
# std.lv = TRUE: fixes factor variances to 1, so phi values ARE correlations
fit_wald <- cfa(
  model  = dvi_model,
  data   = items_df,
  std.lv = TRUE      # ← IMPORTANT: without this, phi is not a correlation
)

# Check that the model converged and fits reasonably
summary(fit_wald, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
```

**Wald confidence intervals.** A positive DVI whose CI excludes zero is evidence for discriminant validity; near-zero, negative, or CI-crossing-zero values are not.

```{r dvi-wald}
#| code-summary: "▶ Extract DVI estimates (Wald CIs)"
# Extract parameter estimates with 95% Wald confidence intervals
pe_wald <- parameterEstimates(fit_wald, level = 0.95)

# Filter to the derived parameters (DVI, CR, and the factor correlation)
key_params <- c("phi_EC_GPI", "CR_EC", "CR_GPI",
                "DVI_1", "DVI_CR_EC", "DVI_CR_GPI")

dvi_wald_table <- pe_wald |>
  filter(label %in% key_params) |>
  select(label, est, se, ci.lower, ci.upper, pvalue) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

kable(
  dvi_wald_table,
  col.names = c("Parameter", "Estimate", "SE", "CI Lower", "CI Upper", "p-value"),
  caption   = "DVI Results with Wald 95% Confidence Intervals"
)
```

**Bootstrap confidence intervals.** Wald CIs rely on asymptotic normality and can be off for constrained parameters. Bootstrap CIs resample the data, refit the CFA, and take percentiles of the DVI values. Report both; use B ≥ 2,000 for a final analysis.

```{r dvi-bootstrap, cache=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "▶ Re-fit with bootstrap SEs (~60 sec)"
# Fit the model again with bootstrap standard errors
# bootstrap = 1000 is a reasonable minimum; use 2000+ for final reporting
set.seed(31415927)
fit_boot <- cfa(
  model     = dvi_model,
  data      = items_df,
  std.lv    = TRUE,
  se        = "bootstrap",   # switch from Wald to bootstrap
  bootstrap = 1000           # number of bootstrap resamples
)

# Extract parameter estimates with percentile bootstrap CIs
pe_boot <- parameterEstimates(
  fit_boot,
  boot.ci.type = "perc",   # percentile method (most commonly recommended)
  level        = 0.95
)

dvi_boot_table <- pe_boot |>
  filter(label %in% key_params) |>
  select(label, est, ci.lower, ci.upper) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

kable(
  dvi_boot_table,
  col.names = c("Parameter", "Estimate", "Bootstrap CI Lower", "Bootstrap CI Upper"),
  caption   = "DVI Results with Percentile Bootstrap 95% Confidence Intervals (B = 1,000)"
)
```

**Forest plot.** A CI that crosses the dashed zero line means discriminant validity is not supported.

```{r dvi-forest-plot, fig.height = 5}
#| code-summary: "▶ Plot: DVI forest plot"
# Build a plotting data frame from the bootstrap results
dvi_plot_df <- dvi_boot_table |>
  filter(label %in% c("DVI_1", "DVI_CR_EC", "DVI_CR_GPI")) |>
  mutate(
    label_nice = case_when(
      label == "DVI_1"      ~ "DVI₁: Phi criterion\n(1 – |φ|)",
      label == "DVI_CR_EC"  ~ "DVI_CR (EC): CR criterion\n(√CR_EC – |φ|)",
      label == "DVI_CR_GPI" ~ "DVI_CR (GPI): CR criterion\n(√CR_GPI – |φ|)"
    ),
    supported = ci.lower > 0   # TRUE if entire CI is above zero
  )

ggplot(dvi_plot_df, aes(x = est, y = reorder(label_nice, est), colour = supported)) +
  # CI bar
  geom_segment(aes(x = ci.lower, xend = ci.upper,
                   y = reorder(label_nice, est), yend = reorder(label_nice, est)),
               linewidth = 1.5) +
  # Point estimate
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  # Zero line (the null: no discriminant validity)
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  # Colour: green = supported, red = not supported
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE"  = "#2c7bb6",
                                 "FALSE" = "#d7191c"),
                      labels = c("TRUE"  = "DV supported (CI > 0)",
                                 "FALSE" = "DV NOT supported (CI ≤ 0)"),
                      name   = NULL) +
  labs(
    x        = "DVI Estimate (with 95% Bootstrap CI)",
    y        = NULL,
    title    = "DVI Forest Plot: EC ↔ GPI Pair",
    subtitle = "If the CI bar crosses the dashed line (0), discriminant validity is not supported"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

**The decision procedure.** Work through it in order.

```{r decision-table}
#| code-summary: "▶ Two-step decision table"
# Determine outcomes based on bootstrap CIs
dvi_results <- dvi_boot_table |>
  filter(label %in% c("DVI_1", "DVI_CR_EC", "DVI_CR_GPI")) |>
  mutate(
    significant = ci.lower > 0,
    verdict     = if_else(significant, "Supported ✓", "Not supported ✗")
  ) |>
  select(label, est, ci.lower, ci.upper, verdict)

kable(
  dvi_results,
  col.names = c("DVI Metric", "Estimate", "95% CI Lower", "95% CI Upper", "Verdict"),
  caption   = "Two-Step Decision Summary for the EC–GPI Pair"
)
```

- **Step 1 (DVI₁ > 0?)** If not, EC and GPI are statistically indistinguishable and cannot be treated as separate constructs.
- **Step 2 (DVI_CR > 0 for both scales?)** If yes, discriminant validity is fully supported. If only one scale passes, the problem is asymmetric and the weaker scale's items are too close to the other construct. If neither passes, you cannot draw clean conclusions about which construct your DV measures.

In our data φ is 0.93, so Step 1 barely passes (or fails) and Step 2 fails for at least one scale, likely both.
:::::

### Comparing the Two Methods

```{r comparison-table}
#| code-summary: "▶ HTMT vs. DVI side-by-side summary"
# Assemble phi and HTMT values for the comparison table
phi_est     <- round(dvi_boot_table$est[dvi_boot_table$label == "phi_EC_GPI"], 3)
phi_ci_lo   <- round(dvi_boot_table$ci.lower[dvi_boot_table$label == "phi_EC_GPI"], 3)
phi_ci_hi   <- round(dvi_boot_table$ci.upper[dvi_boot_table$label == "phi_EC_GPI"], 3)
htmt_val    <- round(get_htmt(htmt_mat, "EC", "GPI"), 3)

comparison <- data.frame(
  Feature         = c("What it tests",
                      "Key output",
                      "Threshold / decision rule",
                      "Accounts for reliability?",
                      "Formal statistical test?",
                      "EC ↔ GPI result"),
  HTMT            = c("Between-scale vs. within-scale correlations",
                      paste0("HTMT2 = ", htmt_val),
                      "< 0.85 (strict) or < 0.90 (lenient)",
                      "No",
                      "No — rule of thumb only",
                      if_else(htmt_val >= 0.90, "FAILED ✗ (≥ 0.90)", "OK ✓")),
  `DVI (Pieters et al., 2025)` = c("Factor correlation and scale reliability",
                      paste0("φ = ", phi_est, " [", phi_ci_lo, ", ", phi_ci_hi, "]"),
                      "DVI > 0 with CI excluding zero",
                      "Yes — uses Congeneric Reliability",
                      "Yes — bootstrap CIs",
                      "See DVI table above")
)

kable(
  comparison,
  col.names = c("Feature", "HTMT", "DVI (Pieters et al., 2025)"),
  caption   = "Comparing the two discriminant validity methods"
)
```

### What to Do When Discriminant Validity Fails

1. **Reconceptualise**: are the constructs genuinely different, or two facets of one?
2. **Revise the scale**: remove or rewrite items too close in meaning to the other construct, and re-collect.
3. **Combine the scales**: if they cannot be separated, treat them as one broader construct (e.g., "pro-environmental orientation").
4. **Report transparently**: at minimum, report the failure and what it implies for interpreting your effects.

::: {.callout-important}
## The core take-home message

An effect on a GPI scale that fails discriminant validity from EC is not clearly interpretable. You cannot claim the campaign increased *purchase intention* if the scale is indistinguishable from *environmental concern*. Discriminant validity testing is a prerequisite for meaningful inference about relationships between constructs.
:::

## Other Methods for Assessing Discriminant Validity

- **Average Variance Extracted (Fornell & Larcker, 1981):** compare the square root of each construct's AVE with its inter-construct correlations. It was dominant before HTMT but is often too lenient.
- **Multitrait-multimethod analysis (Campbell & Fiske, 1959):** measure several traits with several methods and examine the pattern of correlations. Resource-intensive, but the gold standard.
- **Network psychometrics:** Gaussian graphical models make discriminant validity failures visible as dense cross-scale connections.

## Validity Testing for Non-Likert Data {#sec-nonlikert}

The CTT equation, observed = true + error, is a property of *measurement itself*, not of Likert scales. A willingness-to-pay (WTP) response of \$20 might reflect true utility of \$15 plus \$5 of upward error from luxury packaging that inflated perceived market price. A text response of "fine" carries different sentiment depending on who wrote it. In every case the observed signal blends several latent sources:

$$X_\text{observed} = T_\text{true construct} + \lambda \cdot T_\text{other construct} + \varepsilon_\text{random}.$$

The failure mode is identical across formats; what changes is the *tools available to diagnose it*. HTMT and DVI don't apply to WTP, choices, or text, but the question they answer, *is this measure specific enough to support causal inference?*, applies universally. The two worked examples below are in dropdowns.

### Willingness to Pay Data {#sec-wtp}

WTP is meant to capture personal utility, but responses also reflect *perceived market price*. Utility and price belief are conceptually distinct but entangled in one number: $X_\text{WTP} = T_\text{eco utility} + \lambda \cdot T_\text{perceived price} + \varepsilon$. The worked example gives each participant WTP for six eco-cleaning products, three in plain packaging and three in luxury metallic packaging (a cue that should raise perceived price without changing eco-utility). If WTP for luxury products rises while liking and forced choice barely move, WTP is blending utility with price beliefs.

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked example: WTP (simulation, EFA, CFA model comparison, validity checks)

```{r wtp-setup}
#| code-summary: "▶ Simulate WTP data: eco utility vs. perceived price confound"
set.seed(2025)
N_wtp <- 300

# Two latent constructs
eco_utility  <- rnorm(N_wtp, 0, 1)
# Price belief correlated with utility: eco-conscious consumers expect eco products to cost more
price_belief <- 0.40 * eco_utility + rnorm(N_wtp, 0, sqrt(1 - 0.40^2))

# Products 1–3: plain packaging — WTP driven primarily by eco utility
# Products 4–6: luxury packaging — WTP also inflated by price belief
# Log-scale WTP ensures positive values and stabilises variance (currency is right-skewed)
wtp_df <- data.frame(
  plain1 = round(exp(3.0 + 0.70 * eco_utility + 0.15 * price_belief + rnorm(N_wtp, 0, 0.30))),
  plain2 = round(exp(3.0 + 0.72 * eco_utility + 0.12 * price_belief + rnorm(N_wtp, 0, 0.30))),
  plain3 = round(exp(3.0 + 0.68 * eco_utility + 0.18 * price_belief + rnorm(N_wtp, 0, 0.30))),
  lux4   = round(exp(3.0 + 0.40 * eco_utility + 0.60 * price_belief + rnorm(N_wtp, 0, 0.30))),
  lux5   = round(exp(3.0 + 0.38 * eco_utility + 0.62 * price_belief + rnorm(N_wtp, 0, 0.30))),
  lux6   = round(exp(3.0 + 0.42 * eco_utility + 0.58 * price_belief + rnorm(N_wtp, 0, 0.30)))
)
log_wtp_df <- as.data.frame(log(wtp_df))
colnames(log_wtp_df) <- paste0("log_", names(wtp_df))

cat("Mean WTP by packaging type:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Plain packaging (products 1–3): $%.1f\n", mean(unlist(wtp_df[,1:3]))))
cat(sprintf("  Luxury packaging (products 4–6): $%.1f\n", mean(unlist(wtp_df[,4:6]))))
```

**Convergent validity: EFA on log-WTP.** If plain-packaging WTP is driven by eco-utility, those items should load together; luxury items tapping price belief should load on a separate factor.

```{r wtp-efa, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=8}
#| code-summary: "▶ EFA on log-WTP: do plain and luxury products cluster separately?"
wtp_efa <- fa(log_wtp_df, nfactors = 2, rotate = "oblimin", fm = "ml")
print(loadings(wtp_efa), cutoff = 0.30)
```

A clean split into plain and luxury factors means the two sets of WTP responses are driven by different latent sources, the discriminant validity failure made visible in factor-analytic terms.

**Discriminant validity: compare latent models.** For WTP the equivalent of HTMT and DVI is *confirmatory model comparison*: fit CFAs that assume different numbers of latent sources and see which fits better.

```{r wtp-cfa-models}
#| code-summary: "▶ CFA model comparison: 1-factor vs. 2-factor WTP"
# Model 1: All six WTP products driven by a single latent utility construct
wtp_1f <- '
  utility =~ log_plain1 + log_plain2 + log_plain3 +
             log_lux4   + log_lux5   + log_lux6
'

# Model 2: Two latent sources — eco utility (plain) and price-inflated utility (luxury)
wtp_2f <- '
  eco_util  =~ log_plain1 + log_plain2 + log_plain3
  price_wtp =~ log_lux4   + log_lux5   + log_lux6
'

fit_wtp_1f <- cfa(wtp_1f, data = log_wtp_df, std.lv = TRUE)
fit_wtp_2f <- cfa(wtp_2f, data = log_wtp_df, std.lv = TRUE)

fi_1f <- fitMeasures(fit_wtp_1f, c("cfi","rmsea","srmr"))
fi_2f <- fitMeasures(fit_wtp_2f, c("cfi","rmsea","srmr"))

wtp_compare <- data.frame(
  Model   = c("1-factor (single utility construct)",
               "2-factor (eco utility + price belief)"),
  CFI     = round(c(fi_1f["cfi"],   fi_2f["cfi"]),   3),
  RMSEA   = round(c(fi_1f["rmsea"], fi_2f["rmsea"]), 3),
  SRMR    = round(c(fi_1f["srmr"],  fi_2f["srmr"]),  3)
)
kable(wtp_compare,
      col.names = c("Model","CFI","RMSEA","SRMR"),
      caption   = "WTP model comparison: fit indices")

# Likelihood ratio test
print(lavTestLRT(fit_wtp_1f, fit_wtp_2f))
```

If the 2-factor model fits substantially better (higher CFI, lower RMSEA and SRMR, significant likelihood-ratio test), plain and luxury WTP are not measuring the same construct. If a green marketing treatment raises WTP, you cannot cleanly claim it raised eco-utility; it may have made the product seem more premium.

**Two checks without a full model.**

- **Known-groups test:** committed environmental activists should show higher WTP for *plain*-packaged eco products, but similar WTP to non-activists for *luxury* products if the luxury cue moves price beliefs rather than utility.
- **Experimental falsification:** manipulate something that should move price beliefs but not utility (luxury packaging, an inflated "RRP" anchor, a prestige brand cue). If WTP shifts more than liking or forced choice, WTP is contaminated by price beliefs.

The gold standard is a **multitrait-multimethod** design: eco-utility measured by open-ended WTP, liking ratings, forced choice, an incentivised BDM bid, or observed purchase. Convergent validity holds when the same construct appears across methods; discriminant validity holds when eco-utility measures are more similar to each other than to measures of perceived price or brand prestige.
:::::

### Textual Data {#sec-text}

The word "fine" means different things in a British review, an American survey, or a rushed response: $X_\text{text} = T_\text{intended construct} + \lambda \cdot T_\text{context / register / fatigue} + \varepsilon$. When you extract a "green purchase intention" signal from open-ended text, it must be specific to purchase intention and not merely general environmental rhetoric. Topic modeling (LDA, STM) is to text what factor analysis is to Likert items, and it can be used to assess whether the constructs it uncovers are specific enough to support causal claims.

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked example: text topics vs. Likert scales (MTMM)

Suppose participants also wrote brief open-ended responses and you fit a 3-topic STM hoping to recover EC-text, GPI-text, and BA-text. **Convergent validity:** does GPI-text correlate most strongly with the GPI Likert scale? **Discriminant validity:** is the GPI-text vocabulary *distinct* from EC-text, or dominated by environmental language ("sustainable," "eco," "planet")?

```{r text-mtmm}
#| code-summary: "▶ MTMM correlations: text topics vs. Likert scales (two scenarios)"
# In practice you would:
#   1. Collect open-ended responses
#   2. Fit a 3-topic STM: stm(documents, vocab, K=3, prevalence=~condition, data=meta)
#   3. Extract per-participant topic proportions (the theta matrix)
#   4. Correlate theta columns with the corresponding Likert scale scores

# Below we simulate what those MTMM correlations look like
# under two scenarios: clean validity vs. discriminant validity failure

set.seed(42)
ec_score  <- rowMeans(df[, c("EC1","EC2","EC3","EC4")])
gpi_score <- rowMeans(df[, c("GPI1","GPI2","GPI3","GPI4")])
ba_score  <- rowMeans(df[, c("BA1","BA2","BA3")])

# Scenario A: text topics cleanly recover the three intended constructs
ec_text_A  <- 0.65 * ec_score  + 0.10 * gpi_score + 0.05 * ba_score + rnorm(400, 0, 0.5)
gpi_text_A <- 0.10 * ec_score  + 0.62 * gpi_score + 0.08 * ba_score + rnorm(400, 0, 0.5)
ba_text_A  <- 0.08 * ec_score  + 0.07 * gpi_score + 0.60 * ba_score + rnorm(400, 0, 0.5)

# Scenario B: GPI-text is dominated by environmental language (EC-contaminated)
ec_text_B  <- 0.65 * ec_score  + 0.10 * gpi_score + 0.05 * ba_score + rnorm(400, 0, 0.5)
gpi_text_B <- 0.58 * ec_score  + 0.20 * gpi_score + 0.07 * ba_score + rnorm(400, 0, 0.5) # ← failure
ba_text_B  <- 0.08 * ec_score  + 0.07 * gpi_score + 0.60 * ba_score + rnorm(400, 0, 0.5)

# MTMM correlation tables (text rows × Likert columns)
mtmm_A <- round(cor(
  data.frame(EC_Likert=ec_score, GPI_Likert=gpi_score, BA_Likert=ba_score,
             EC_text=ec_text_A, GPI_text=gpi_text_A, BA_text=ba_text_A)
)[4:6, 1:3], 2)

mtmm_B <- round(cor(
  data.frame(EC_Likert=ec_score, GPI_Likert=gpi_score, BA_Likert=ba_score,
             EC_text=ec_text_B, GPI_text=gpi_text_B, BA_text=ba_text_B)
)[4:6, 1:3], 2)

cat("Scenario A — Good discriminant validity (text topics recover constructs cleanly):\n")
print(mtmm_A)
cat("\nScenario B — Discriminant validity failure (GPI-text bleeds into EC):\n")
print(mtmm_B)
```

Each row is a text measure, each column a Likert measure. **Diagonal** entries are convergent validity correlations and should be the highest in each row; **off-diagonal** entries are discriminant checks and should be noticeably lower. In Scenario A, GPI-text correlates most with GPI-Likert. In Scenario B it correlates almost as strongly with EC-Likert: a treatment effect on this text measure could reflect more willingness to buy or simply more environmental language.

Two diagnostics are specific to topic models. **Topic exclusivity** (the FREX metric in STM) asks whether each topic has distinctive vocabulary, the analogue of item specificity. **Topic correlations** (`topicCorr()`) are the analogue of the factor correlation φ: topic scores correlating at 0.93 is quantitatively the same failure as φ = 0.93 between latent factors.
:::::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Summary: validity assessment across data types

| | Likert scales | WTP | Text |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Convergent validity** | EFA loadings, CFA fit, α | EFA/CFA on log-WTP | Text–Likert MTMM correlations |
| **Discriminant validity** | HTMT, DVI | CFA model comparison, falsification | Topic exclusivity, topic correlations |
| **Gold standard design** | MTMM across methods | MTMM (WTP + liking + choice) | MTMM (text + Likert + behavior) |
| **Key failure mode** | EC–GPI cross-loading | Price belief contamination | Environmental language in GPI topic |

Regardless of data type, ask: *what else, besides my intended construct, could plausibly move this measure?*
:::

## When You Have Only One DV: Discriminant Validity as an Identification Problem {#sec-single-dv-identification}

Everything so far needed several indicators per construct. Many DVs have one: a single WTP number, a single choice, a single behavior. With one observed variable there is nothing to run HTMT or DVI on, and no statistical test can pull apart two latent sources that enter one number. In econometric terms this is an **identification problem**: one equation, two unknowns. The data alone cannot say how much of a WTP response is "value" and how much is something else.

That does not remove the researcher's responsibility to establish discriminant validity. It changes the tool, from a statistical test to an **argument from the data-generating process**. Use theory to write down what produces the number, name the other latent variables that could move it, and then use the design to supply the independent variation the single measure lacks.

### Step 1: Write down the data-generating process

Willingness to pay is typically used as a measure of people's latent *value* for a product. But WTP also captures a related, psychologically differentiable construct: people's **price expectations**. [Evangelidis, Jung, and Moon (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1002/arcp.1103) review evidence that a hypothetical WTP question leads respondents to imagine themselves as buyers even when they would never buy, and that their answers tend to track the perceived *market price* of the good: respondents effectively ask "what does this typically cost?" as much as "what is it worth to me?" Vegans, for example, state non-zero WTP for a steak. Writing this as a data-generating process:

$$\text{WTP} = \alpha + \lambda_V \cdot \text{Value} + \lambda_P \cdot \text{PriceExpectation} + \varepsilon .$$

Value and price expectations are *related* (eco-conscious consumers expect eco products to cost more), which is what makes this a discriminant validity problem and not random noise. Other candidate contaminants include strategic bidding (buyers shading WTP below their valuation to get a good deal), hypothetical bias (overstating when nothing is at stake), and budget constraints. Which of these threaten *your* inference depends on whether they differ across your conditions or predictors.

### Step 2: Ask what independent variation the design can supply

Because the single number cannot separate the sources, the separation has to come from outside it:

| Strategy | What it does | Example with WTP |
|---|---|---|
| **Measure the rival construct** | Observe the contaminant directly and test whether your treatment moves it | Ask "what would this typically cost?" and compare conditions. Don't simply control for it: measured after treatment, it is an outcome of treatment |
| **Manipulate the rival construct** | Move it while leaving the target construct unchanged | Vary a reference price or typical-price cue; if WTP moves, price expectations are in the number |
| **Use groups where one component is near zero** | Any response there must come from the other component | Non-dog owners and a dog toy, vegans and a steak: positive WTP reveals the price-expectation component |
| **Change the elicitation** | Close off the route the contaminant uses | An explicit "would not buy" option, or an incentive-compatible procedure such as BDM (which has its own strategic issues) |
| **Triangulate with other measures** | Use measures with different contaminants | Choice, liking ratings, and a consequential valuation; see {{< ref sec-single-dv style="long" >}} |

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## A small simulation: why the data alone can't separate them, and what a design-based check adds

An eco-label is randomly assigned. By construction it does **not** change personal value; it only raises expected price. A second factor randomly shows participants a high reference price. The single DV is WTP.

```{r sdv-sim}
#| code-summary: "▶ Simulate: one DV (WTP), two latent sources"

sdv <- local({
  set.seed(2025)
  n      <- 2000
  label  <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)                    # eco-label (randomised)
  cue    <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)                    # high reference-price cue (randomised)
  value  <- rnorm(n)                             # latent personal value: the label does NOT change it
  pexp   <- 0.4 * value + 0.5 * label + 0.5 * cue + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(1 - 0.4^2))   # latent price expectation
  wtp    <- 0.8 * value + 0.6 * pexp + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)                            # the single observed DV
  pexp_m <- pexp + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)              # noisy self-report: "what would this typically cost?"
  data.frame(label, cue, value, pexp, wtp, pexp_m)
})

fit_a <- lm(wtp ~ label + cue, data = sdv)
fit_m <- lm(pexp_m ~ label + cue, data = sdv)    # does the label move the measured price expectation?
fit_v <- lm(value ~ label + cue, data = sdv)     # the truth, available only because this is a simulation
cf <- function(fit, term) summary(fit)$coefficients[term, 1:2]
fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f (SE %.2f)", x[1], x[2])

sdv_tab <- data.frame(
  Check = c("Effect of the label on WTP",
            "Effect of the price cue on WTP",
            "Effect of the label on the measured expected-price item",
            "True effect of the label on value (known only in a simulation)"),
  Estimate = c(fmt(cf(fit_a, "label")), fmt(cf(fit_a, "cue")), fmt(cf(fit_m, "label")), fmt(cf(fit_v, "label"))),
  Reading = c("Looks like the label raised value, but WTP alone can't say why",
              "WTP moves with a cue meant to change only the market price, so WTP carries a price-expectation component",
              "The label also raises expected price: a rival route to the same WTP increase",
              "Zero by construction"))
kable(sdv_tab, caption = "One DV, two latent sources")

# The simulated truth: label raises WTP only through price expectation (0.6 x 0.5 = 0.30)
stopifnot(abs(cf(fit_a, "label")[1] - 0.30) < 4 * cf(fit_a, "label")[2],
          abs(cf(fit_a, "cue")[1]   - 0.30) < 4 * cf(fit_a, "cue")[2],
          abs(cf(fit_v, "label")[1]) < 4 * cf(fit_v, "label")[2],
          abs(cf(fit_m, "label")[1] - 0.50) < 4 * cf(fit_m, "label")[2])
```

Reading the table: the label raises WTP, which looks like evidence that it raised *value*, but WTP alone cannot tell us why. A measured expected-price item shows the label also moves price expectations, a rival route to the same WTP increase. And the randomized price-information cue, designed to change only the market-price cue, moves WTP too, so WTP carries a price-expectation component. Neither check is a statistical test on the single DV; both come from the design.
:::::

### Step 3: State what you can and cannot claim

Report the claim the design identifies. "The label raised stated WTP" is supported by randomization. "The label raised consumers' *value* for the product" additionally requires evidence that price expectations did not drive the result. If you cannot supply that evidence, scope the claim to the observed DV, say which rival constructs remain open, and say which design feature (a measured expectation item, a price-cue manipulation, an incentive-compatible follow-up) would close them. This is the same logic as {{< ref sec-single-dv style="long" >}}, applied to discriminant validity: there, the question was whether the reporting relationship differs across groups; here, it is whether the number measures one construct at all.

---

# Interlude: Reliability Is Not Validity {#sec-reliability-validity}

## The Core Distinction

The sections above showed how to detect discriminant validity failures. A related failure trips up researchers constantly: **a scale can be highly reliable and still be invalid.**

**Reliability** is *consistency*: do the items within a scale hang together? Cronbach's alpha, the most common index, is computed entirely *within* a scale:

$$\alpha = \frac{k\,\bar{\rho}}{1 + (k-1)\,\bar{\rho}},$$

where $k$ is the number of items and $\bar{\rho}$ is the average inter-item correlation within the scale. Nothing in it refers to other constructs, so alpha is blind to discriminant validity by design. A scale can have alpha = 0.95 and an HTMT of 1.20: perfectly reliable at measuring something indistinguishable from another construct.

The Spearman–Brown prophecy makes it worse: **adding items always raises alpha**, whether or not the new items tap your construct or an adjacent one. Researchers who respond to low alpha by writing more items can push alpha up while discriminant validity erodes. The consequences are inflated correlations between constructs, uninterpretable regression and mediation coefficients, and results that replicate reliably but mean little.

## Interactive Simulator: Reliability vs. Discriminant Validity

Use the controls to see how alpha and HTMT respond *independently* to changes in scale properties.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What to try

1. **Add items and watch alpha climb while HTMT stays flat.** Go from 4 to 12 items: alpha rises from moderate to excellent; HTMT does not move.
2. **The "looks great, is broken" scenario.** 8 items, within-correlation 0.55, between-correlation 0.50: alpha = 0.91 (excellent) but HTMT = 0.91 (violated). This is common in sustainability, well-being, and attitude research.
3. **Set within = between.** Alpha is unchanged; HTMT reaches 1.0.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| code-fold: false
viewof sim_k = Inputs.range([2, 15], {
  step: 1, value: 4,
  label: "Number of items per scale (k)"
})
viewof sim_within_r = Inputs.range([0.10, 0.95], {
  step: 0.01, value: 0.50,
  label: "Within-scale inter-item correlation (ρ̄)"
})
viewof sim_between_r = Inputs.range([0.00, 0.95], {
  step: 0.01, value: 0.30,
  label: "Between-scale correlation (discriminant validity threat)"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| code-fold: false
rel_alpha = (sim_k * sim_within_r) / (1 + (sim_k - 1) * sim_within_r)
rel_htmt  = sim_between_r / sim_within_r

alpha_col = rel_alpha >= 0.70 ? "#2a9d8f" : "#e63946"
htmt_col  = rel_htmt  <  0.85 ? "#2a9d8f"
           : rel_htmt  <  0.90 ? "#e9c46a"
           : "#e63946"

alpha_label = rel_alpha >= 0.90 ? "Excellent"
            : rel_alpha >= 0.80 ? "Good"
            : rel_alpha >= 0.70 ? "Acceptable"
            : "Too low"

htmt_label = rel_htmt < 0.85 ? "✓ Discriminant validity supported"
           : rel_htmt < 0.90 ? "⚠ Borderline — approaching threshold"
           : "✗ Discriminant validity VIOLATED"

html`<div style="display:flex;gap:16px;flex-wrap:wrap;margin:16px 0;">
  <div style="flex:1;min-width:200px;border:2px solid ${alpha_col};border-radius:8px;padding:16px;text-align:center;background:${alpha_col}18;">
    <div style="font-size:.8em;color:#555;text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:.05em;">Cronbach's Alpha</div>
    <div style="font-size:2.4em;font-weight:700;color:${alpha_col};">${rel_alpha.toFixed(3)}</div>
    <div style="font-size:.9em;color:${alpha_col};font-weight:600;">${alpha_label}</div>
    <div style="font-size:.75em;color:#888;margin-top:4px;">Threshold ≥ 0.70</div>
  </div>
  <div style="flex:1;min-width:200px;border:2px solid ${htmt_col};border-radius:8px;padding:16px;text-align:center;background:${htmt_col}18;">
    <div style="font-size:.8em;color:#555;text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:.05em;">HTMT</div>
    <div style="font-size:2.4em;font-weight:700;color:${htmt_col};">${rel_htmt.toFixed(3)}</div>
    <div style="font-size:.9em;color:${htmt_col};font-weight:600;">${htmt_label}</div>
    <div style="font-size:.75em;color:#888;margin-top:4px;">Threshold < 0.85</div>
  </div>
</div>`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| code-fold: false
//| fig-cap: "Cronbach's alpha climbs with each additional item (blue). HTMT is completely unaffected (red). Dashed lines show common decision thresholds. The two metrics are measuring entirely different things."

k_vals = Array.from({length: 14}, (_, i) => i + 2)

alpha_long = k_vals.flatMap(k => [
  {k, metric: "Cronbach's α", value: (k * sim_within_r) / (1 + (k - 1) * sim_within_r)},
  {k, metric: "HTMT",         value: sim_between_r / sim_within_r}
])

Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 280,
  marginLeft: 55, marginRight: 20, marginTop: 20, marginBottom: 40,
  color: {
    legend: true,
    domain: ["Cronbach's α", "HTMT"],
    range:  ["#457b9d",      "#e63946"]
  },
  x: {label: "Items per scale (k)", tickValues: [2,4,6,8,10,12,14,15]},
  y: {
    label: "Value",
    domain: [0, Math.min(1.3, Math.max(1.1, rel_htmt + 0.15))]
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0.70], {stroke: "#f4a261", strokeDasharray: "5,3", strokeWidth: 1.4}),
    Plot.ruleY([0.85], {stroke: "#e63946", strokeDasharray: "5,3", strokeWidth: 1.4}),
    Plot.line(alpha_long, {x: "k", y: "value", stroke: "metric", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot(alpha_long.filter(d => d.k === sim_k),
             {x: "k", y: "value", fill: "metric", r: 7})
  ]
})
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The bottom line

A high alpha confirms your items measure *something* consistently. It does not confirm that the something is your intended construct or that it is distinct from adjacent constructs.
:::

---

## Researcher Checklist: Discriminant Validity {#sec-checklist-discriminant-validity}

::: {.callout-note}
## Key questions before using your scales

- [ ] **Does each measured scale correspond to a single latent dimension?** Items should load strongly on one factor and weakly on all others (cross-loadings < 0.30).
- [ ] **Do you have evidence that your constructs are empirically distinct?** HTMT < 0.85 for all construct pairs is the standard threshold. A high Cronbach's alpha does not answer this question.
- [ ] **If HTMT is high, is the problem in the items or in the theory?** High cross-loadings mean contaminated items; a high factor correlation may mean theoretically redundant constructs.
- [ ] **Will discriminant validity failure bias your downstream analysis?** Two discriminantly invalid predictors in one regression produce unstable coefficients; a mediator that overlaps with the outcome inflates indirect effects.
- [ ] **If you have only one DV (WTP, a choice, a behavior), have you written down its data-generating process?** Name the other latent variables that could move it, and the design feature (a measure, a manipulation, a comparison group) that rules each one out.
:::
